The Ruy Lopez at 800, 1200 and 1600: the same three moves, understood three different ways. ♟️

Which level are you playing it at? 👇

ig_caption:
The Ruy Lopez, also called the Spanish, is named after a 16th-century Spanish priest who wrote about it. It is one opening you can play for life, because what you understand in it grows with you.

At 800: Bb5 attacks the knight that guards e5, but Bxc6 and Nxe5 doesn't win a pawn yet, because ...Qd4 wins it back.
At 1200: after ...a6 the bishop drops to a4, and White castles, leaving e4 on purpose.
At 1600: the Closed Ruy. c3 prepares d4, h3 stops ...Bg4, and the knight takes the long road to g3.

slides.title: Why it's called the Spanish
slides.body: It is named after Ruy López de Segura, a Spanish priest who wrote about it in his chess book of 1561. Five centuries on, it is still played at every level.
slides.note: Learn it once, and it keeps teaching you as you improve.

slides.title: At 800: the idea
slides.take: White's bishop attacks the knight on c6, the piece that guards the e5 pawn. That pressure is the whole point of the opening.
slides.edge: It isn't a free pawn yet: after 3...a6 4.Bxc6 dxc6 5.Nxe5?, Black plays 5...Qd4 and wins it back.

slides.title: At 1200: the timing
slides.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O
slides.take: 3...a6 asks the bishop a question; 4.Ba4 keeps the pressure. Then White castles and leaves the e4 pawn undefended, on purpose.
slides.edge: If Black takes on e4, that is the Open Variation: a real line, but White gets active play and usually regains the pawn.

slides.title: At 1600: the plan
slides.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3
slides.take: The Closed Ruy is slow on purpose. c3 prepares d4, and h3 stops ...Bg4 from pinning the knight on f3.
slides.edge: Next comes the Ruy's signature manoeuvre: the b1 knight walks d2, f1 and g3, joining the kingside.

slides.title: Every level you climb
slides.title2: is a line on the poster.
